migrationNotes: Spine: start with a hallway of two lamps, count every setting, ask a sentence of each setting (and, then or), and finish by using the rows to test a piece of reasoning.
The first figure is the p → q table from the previous lessons, relabelled with the lamps; the 'and' and 'or' tables stay hidden until the learner has predicted.
Left out of the lesson (still in the course): building-a-truth-table-rows-check, building-a-truth-table-inclusive-check.

lesson.title: Building a truth table

lead.text: Treat the lamps as two claims. Let p be “Lamp 1 is on” and let q be “Lamp 2 is on”. Each lamp is on or off, so p is true or false and q is true or false. A state of the hallway is a choice of true or false for both, written with two letters. TT means both lamps are on, and TF means lamp 1 is on and lamp 2 is off.

To list every state without gaps, fix lamp 1 first and pair it with both settings of lamp 2, then do the same with lamp 1 off. That gives four rows: TT, TF, FT and FF. Two choices for the first lamp, each paired with two for the second, make 2 × 2 rows. Each extra lamp would double the list. A list that skips a pairing, or repeats one, is wrong.

afterFigure.text: A list of every row, with the value of a sentence beside each, is called a truth table. The one above gives the value of “If lamp 1 is on, then lamp 2 is on”, which is p → q, the conditional from the if-then lesson. It is false in a single row. The rest of the lesson builds tables for two other sentences.

diagram.outputLabel: If lamp 1 is on, lamp 2 is on

lead.text: The hallway has two lamps, and each one is either on or off.

steps.headline: Testing a sentence in every row

lead.text: A table earns its keep when you ask it about a sentence. Take “Lamp 1 is on and lamp 2 is on”. In symbols that is p ∧ q, where ∧ reads “and”. The sentence is a claim, so each row gives it a truth value, and to find the value you ask whether the sentence describes the state in that row correctly.

Go row by row. The row TT describes lamps that are both on, so the sentence describes it correctly. For each of the other rows, check the two lamps in turn against the sentence, which needs both of them. Doing this for all four rows fills in a column of values, one for each state. The sentence stays the same from row to row, and only the state it is checked against changes.
The symbol ∧ reads “and”: p ∧ q says that p holds and q holds. Go through the four rows and test it in each.

reveal.text: Compare your count with the table. Only TT survives, because each other row leaves one claim false.

lead.text: The word “or” is slipperier than “and”. A café sign says “Tea or coffee included with breakfast”, and nobody expects to be turned away for taking both. A menu that says “soup or salad” usually means one or the other, and you are expected to choose. The same word is doing two jobs.

Logic settles this once. The symbol ∨ reads “or” and includes the case where both claims hold. The claim p ∨ q is true when at least one of p and q is true, and that includes the case where both are. This reading is called the inclusive or. The other one rules out taking both. It is called exclusive, and we won't use it unless we say so.
Fixing the meaning matters because a table only works when each symbol reads the same way every time. With ∨ settled, any table that uses it can be read the same way.

diagram.alt: Two signs compared over four choices. The inclusive sign tea or coffee allows taking both. The exclusive sign soup or salad does not.
diagram.caption: The inclusive reading and the exclusive reading differ only in the row where both are taken. The course uses the inclusive one.

steps.headline: Using the rows to test reasoning

lead.text: Rows can do more than evaluate a sentence. They can test a piece of reasoning. Suppose we are told two things about p and q and asked what follows. Each row is a possible state of the world, and the facts we are told rule out some of them.

Here is the method with different facts. We know that p ∧ q is false and that p is true. List the four rows. Keep only the rows where p ∧ q is false, which are TF, FT and FF. Then keep only the rows where p is true. That leaves TF, and in TF the claim q is false. In every row that fits what we know, q is false, so q must be false.
The same table also catches bad reasoning. If someone draws a conclusion that fails in even one row that fits the facts, the conclusion doesn't follow. That single row is the proof.

diagram.alt: A four-row table of p, q and p and q. Starting with all rows, the fact that p and q is false rules out one row, and the fact that p is true leaves only the row where p is true and q false.
diagram.caption: Step through the facts. Rows marked ruled out no longer fit what we know. The rows left decide the answer.

lesson.orientation: Enumerate the cases of a two-variable compound statement and read validity off the result.
lesson.nextAction: Separate an argument's conclusion from the claims offered in its support.

blocks.text: A hallway has two lamps, and each lamp is either on or off. A caretaker has to check the wiring and wants to see the hallway in every possible state before signing it off.

That sounds easy until you try to do it without missing one. With the first lamp on, the second might be on or off. With the first lamp off, the second might again be on or off. It is easy to check three states and feel sure you have seen them all. The caretaker needs a way of listing the states that guarantees nothing is skipped and nothing is counted twice.

Logic has such a list, and this lesson builds it. Each lamp becomes a claim, each state becomes a row, and an extra column says what a sentence like “both lamps are on” comes to in that state. We then use the rows to test a piece of reasoning.

intro.promise: By the end you'll list every case for two claims and use the rows to test a piece of reasoning.

recap.keyIdea: A truth table lists every case once. Read along a row to see what a symbol such as ∧ or ∨ does, and look for a row that breaks the reasoning.

blocks.text: You counted the settings of the two lamps, then found how many rows make “and” true and how many make “or” true. You then used the rows to see that “p or q” together with “not p” forces q, and that “p or q” with p true forces nothing about q.

recap.nextHook: The table tests reasoning once the reasoning has been written out. The next lesson starts a step earlier, with an argument in everyday words, and asks which sentence is the conclusion and which are the reasons for it.

questions.prompt: How many different settings can the two lamps have?
hints: Lamp 1 can be on or off. How many settings is that?
Pair each setting of lamp 1 with both settings of lamp 2.
List them: both on, then the three others.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two settings for one lamp times two for the other gives four.

questions.onCorrect: Four: 2 × 2. Every setting of one lamp pairs with both settings of the other.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the settings of one lamp. The second lamp doubles it.
Check the list. Both lamps on is one setting, so what are the others?

questions.prompt: How many rows make p ∧ q true?
hints: The symbol ∧ reads “and”. What does “p and q” need?
Look at TT, TF, FT and FF in turn.
Count only rows with two true inputs.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only the TT row makes both claims true.

questions.onCorrect: One. “p and q” needs both, and only the TT row has both.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what you get if one true claim is enough. ∧ needs both.
Check a row with only one claim true. Does “p and q” hold there?
Go through the four rows one at a time and test “p and q”.

questions.prompt: How many rows make p ∨ q true?
hints: Inclusive ∨ needs at least one true input.
Does the row where both are true count?
Which row is the only one that fails?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At least one claim is true in three of the four rows.

questions.onCorrect: Three. “p or q” holds unless both are false, and in this course it includes the row where both are true.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how many rows make p ∧ q true. Here one true claim is enough.
Rows where both claims are true count too, because ∨ is inclusive.
The row where both claims are false fails.

questions.prompt: Someone reasons: “p or q is true, and p is true, so q must be false.” Which row shows the reasoning goes wrong?
hints: Keep the rows where both starting facts hold.
In one of them q is true. Which?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: With p and q both true, “p or q” and “p” hold, but q is not false.

questions.onCorrect: p true, q true: both facts hold and q is still true. One such row is enough to break the reasoning.

misconceptions.feedback: p is false here, so one of the starting facts fails. Keep only rows where both hold.
p ∨ q is false here, so this row isn't a case the reasoning starts from.

questions.prompt: Three independent claims each have two truth values. How many rows does the table need?
hints: Each extra claim doubles the number of cases.
Two choices for each of three claims.
Multiply the three numbers of choices.
questions.onCorrect: Eight: 2 × 2 × 2. Each new claim doubles the rows.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the choices. Each claim multiplies the cases instead.
That is the rows for two claims. The third claim doubles them.

questions.prompt: Can inclusive p ∨ q be true when both claims are true? Answer yes or no.
hints: The word inclusive matters here.
At least one true claim is enough, so both is allowed.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Inclusive disjunction allows both claims to be true.

questions.onCorrect: Yes. Inclusive “or” needs at least one claim true, and both counts.

misconceptions.feedback: Inclusive “or” doesn't rule out both. What does “inclusive” add?

questions.prompt: Why do we throw away the rows where p is true?
hints: Which facts did we start with?

acceptedIdeas: We were told p is not true, so those rows don't fit.

questions.prompt: A café sign says “Tea or coffee included.” Dev takes both. In the logician's sense, is the sign's claim true? Answer yes or no.
hints: Does the symbol ∨ rule out the case where both hold?
questions.onCorrect: Yes. In logic “or” includes both, so taking both still makes it true.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the everyday reading. The logician's “or” doesn't rule out both.
